name: Blockchain Limitations
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: What Blockchain Still Can't Do, and Why That Isn't Going Away
lesson.summary: Beyond any single failed pilot, blockchain has structural limitations, throughput ceilings, the oracle problem, irreversible errors, and unresolved governance questions, that no amount of better engineering has fully removed, because they follow directly from the same design choices that give blockchain its benefits.
lesson.body:
The previous chapters looked at specific projects that succeeded or failed for business and governance reasons. This chapter is different: it looks at limitations that are structural, meaning they follow from what a blockchain fundamentally is, rather than from how well any particular team executed.

Start with scalability, which this chapter builds on directly. Because every participating node has to verify and store every transaction in order to maintain decentralized trust without a central authority, there is an inherent ceiling on how fast a blockchain can process transactions; Bitcoin processes on the order of a handful of transactions per second, and Ethereum, before various scaling upgrades, handled only somewhat more. This tradeoff is sometimes called the scalability trilemma: decentralization, security, and scalability are in tension, and design choices that improve one tend to cost you another. Newer approaches, including rollups and sharding, push against this ceiling, but they typically do so by adding complexity or by reintroducing some degree of trust in a smaller set of operators, which is worth noting honestly rather than treating scaling upgrades as having simply solved the problem outright.

Energy use is a related but separate issue, and it is important not to overgeneralize it. Proof-of-work systems like Bitcoin secure their ledger by requiring real-world computational effort, which is precisely why they consume large amounts of electricity; that cost is not a bug, it is the mechanism. But it is not true of every blockchain. Ethereum's move to proof of stake in 2022, an upgrade generally referred to as the Merge, cut Ethereum's energy consumption by a very large margin, credible estimates put it above ninety-nine percent, so "blockchain is inherently energy-wasteful" is a claim that applies unevenly depending on which consensus mechanism a specific chain actually uses.

A more subtle limitation is the oracle problem, which connects directly to smart contract risks. A blockchain can guarantee that data has not been altered once it is recorded on the ledger, but it cannot guarantee that the data was true at the moment it was recorded. A smart contract that needs to know a real-world price, a shipment's location, or whether a flight was delayed has to get that information from somewhere outside the blockchain, called an oracle, and that oracle becomes a trust bottleneck the blockchain's own cryptography does nothing to solve. The blunt version of this problem is sometimes summarized as garbage in, gospel out: bad data that makes it onto the ledger becomes just as immutable, and just as trusted by anyone reading it later, as good data.

Immutability itself cuts both ways. It is marketed as a pure benefit, nobody can secretly alter history, but it is also a real liability: a coding bug, a mistaken transaction, or a stolen private key produces an outcome that generally cannot be undone except through the extraordinary and contentious step of the community agreeing to fork the protocol's history, as happened after the 2016 DAO hack on Ethereum, which led to a split between Ethereum and Ethereum Classic. Immutability can also collide with the law directly: data protection regulations like the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation give individuals a right to have their personal data deleted, which is very difficult to honor on a ledger designed specifically so that nothing can be deleted, and it is a major reason regulated personal data, including the healthcare records discussed earlier, generally stays off-chain even in blockchain-based systems.

Finally, governance and key management are unglamorous but real limits. Someone still has to decide how the underlying protocol gets upgraded, and disagreements about that can split a community, as the DAO fork shows. And there is no institutional safety net for an individual's mistakes: a bank can verify your identity and reset a forgotten password, but losing a private key generally means permanently losing whatever it controlled, with no customer service line to call. These are not defects waiting to be patched in a future version. They are direct consequences of removing a central authority, which is the same design choice that gives blockchain its selling points in the first place, so they are unlikely to fully disappear even as the technology matures.
